utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in the courtroom. This is IT-06-90-T, the Prosecutor versus Ante Gotovina et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Before we continue, Mr. Kehoe, Mr. Waespi, were you able to find a solution for P425 marked for identification?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we are and I will tell you the confusion came from it being Gracac as opposed to -- the town and the village, the village is in the Split military district, the town is not and there was some confusion there; but I do believe that we have mutually resolved it and the objections on that score, well we have no objections at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then I take it that where the other parties joined the objection, they also now join in the withdrawal. Then P425 is admitted into evidence. I hardly dare to say about the village and the town but that's clear. We know where the village is we know where the town is. Let's proceed but not, Mr. Marti, after I have reminded you that you are still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony, that is that you will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth. Mr. Kehoe I think at the end of this session, I'll come back to you about timing, et cetera, but please first continue your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Marti and yesterday we were talking about Golubic. Your Honour, if I could just briefly turn it to private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We turn it to private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Marti, were you aware that there was a weapons depot for the ARSK in Golubic?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not clearly aware. I just heard the rumours from other UNMO that there must be something but me, myself, I didn't see anything and I mean for me it looks quite funny, I mean you have a church and then you cover the church with camouflage, but I mean it's still a church so what should be the meaning of cover a church with camouflage. So for me, I didn't actually understand it and I haven't seen anything in Golubic former to Operation Storm.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: In addition to the church, were you aware of a separate weapons depot for the ARSK in Golubic?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't see it by my eyes there before Operation Oluja.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did you hear about it from other UNMOs that there was an ammunitions depot for the ARSK in Golubic?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was some discussions. There might be or they suppose that there is something because before Operation Oluja we didn't have access to all the areas in our zone of where we had to report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So let's talk about Golubic, are you saying that the ARSK did not let you examine military facilities in Golubic?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not only Golubic, it was also, for example, Plavno valley we didn't have access before Operation Oluja to Plavno valley as well as directly to Golubic, for example, to see what is in this church which is covered in camouflage.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That was because the ARSK would not let you; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me show you an excerpt of a document if I may so we can get these numbers correct, we are going to distribute paper copies of this, Judge, and this is a report dated the 22nd of August, 1995 from General Cervenko, the Chief of Staff of the HV. We will get the whole document translated but for the sake of this discussion, we're interested in this one page which we have translated. If we can put that on the ELMO. Mr. Usher, I'm interested in the second paragraph talking about "Up to now ..." This report notes to follows, "Up to now, it is known that numerous depots contain large amounts of ammunition and other weapons. And the discussion is weapons seized after Operation Storm. "For example, in the Stara Straza depot, there were -- almost 15 wagons he is of ammunition which we do not completely dispose of." Do you know where Stara Straza is, Mr. Marti?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I should have looked at my map maybe then I would find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay. We will go up on that map just briefly before we go to this matter on the ELMO, which is D384. This is one of the series of maps that Mr. Misetic used yesterday. And if we can have the English translation there as opposed to the B/C/S translation. You see Knin is down on the lower right-hand corner do you see that, Mr. Marti, and you see that the circle that the Stara Straza barracks are, are you familiar with that location? The red circle on the right-hand side of the page?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it on the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the ARSK barracks in the Stara Straza area?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So I take it based on your answer, you didn't know that they had weapons depot?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Even --

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's basically what I have to say because as I mentioned already, there were some rumours but me, myself, I was not there to have a look at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, in the discussions with other UNMOs, did you learn that there was a weapons depot in Stara Straza?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember this special name Stara Straza.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we can go back to the item on the ELMO. Going down to the next sentence, "In Golubic depot," and I'm talking about the paragraph up to now: "In the Golubic depot in Knin, there is approximately 7.000 tons of ammunition and weapons prepared for arming three brigades. There are various rockets amongst which are type Orcan, Plamen Oganj, large amounts of reserve parts, food, various military equipment and sanitary material. 22 KUB rockets, large amounts of various anti-personnel and anti-tank mines and several tons of explosives were seized. The amounts of ammunition and other assets are several times greater than those used during the operation." Now, you noted for us in your witness statement P415 at page 2 -- excuse me, P416 page 2 that the ARSK was poorly equipped. Were you aware that they had this much equipment in the Golubic amo dump?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not aware but I said poorly equipped because when I remember, for example, a checkpoint, I mean that was the point where we saw the RSK soldiers every day. I mean those checkpoints were very poorly, there was -- for example, the checkpoint between Knin and Drnis, there was a simple -- a camping coach and an old camping coach manned with one man. Even he didn't have -- also on the other checkpoint, they didn't have radio connection with the commanding in Knin, for example, or in Vrlika and for me, this didn't give the impression that they are well equipped, they are well-organised. Even many times I thought but where are the preparations to protect the whole area? I mean when you just pass through the zone of separation, first you pass the Serb checkpoint, then the UN checkpoint then on the other side, the Croatian checkpoint and you can see a very different, for example, how on the Croatian side, their checkpoints were equipped. So that gave me the impression that it must be so well-organised and also sometimes when we were locked on the checkpoint, because they wanted to see a permission or something like that, they couldn't clarify by radio what is the problem. So we had to go back to Knin, get the permission, and come back. So that was my impression.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, just going back to this particular ammunition depot. As a UN Military Observer, is there some reason why you didn't know about this ammunition depot in Golubic in your role as an UNMO?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I came to this Sector South in early -- in middle of June, there were some procedures established where we were allowed to patrol and were not. And for me, it was -- I mean I didn't have personal reason to say to my colleague, come on and let's go to try, for example, to Golubic. I mean it was just normal procedure to Golubic. We are not allowed to go, so we had our daily routes where we patrol. For example, we were allowed up to Strmica but only up to the checkpoint. We were allowed to Otric and we were allowed to go to Drnis.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we can continue on on this page, if we can down just a couple of paragraphs towards the bottom, it's okay, Mr. Usher, we can leave it: "There was likewise a factory in Licki Osik which had numerous items there. 55 tanks, five armoured transporters, 106 various guns, howitzers, et cetera, as well as the last line, 6 MRL type Oganjs. Again, sir, did you patrol the Licki Osik area and were you aware of this depot?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot see where.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It's in the bottom paragraph on the page.

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I mean I don't know the area which you have mentioned. Licki Osik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You are unaware of that area?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know this name so, I should figure out on the map where it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let's turn our attention from Golubic to Strmica --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, at this time we'll offer into evidence this report on Operation Storm. We will provide a full translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I don't object though just an observation. The General signed as in the English translation 4-star General which is a funny way to sign a document and the B/C/S says General Zbora. My B/C/S isn't -- not minimally sufficient but I don't think that means 4 Zbora anyway, the document says what it says; and we perhaps wait until we have a translation of the whole document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. No objections. Therefore, Mr. Registrar ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit D387.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D387 is admitted into evidence. If, however, any of the Defence teams will ask for the complete translation, perhaps they could specifically ask about Zbora I've not no idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Judge, frankly I have no idea either but we will ask for a full translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, with going to Strmica and your trip to Strmica, and just bear with me, Mr. Marti, I'm going to cover some of the subjects that were both in your report as well as what was discussed with Mr. Waespi. Now, you just noted for us there were certain areas that you could not go and you mentioned Strmica being one of them; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mentioned that we were allowed to go on the street up to Strmica, but only up to the checkpoint.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So when you said -- so when you talked about a restriction of movement, you could drive up to the checkpoint and no further?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, when you were going there on the 30th, you were going there at the request of the ARSK, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The request came from ARSK through the HQ in Knin to our team.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And you -- just going through your statement, you went and got an ARSK liaison officer and drove up to Strmica?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was normally the procedure when we came close to the zone of separation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And this liaison officer was going to be your escort to show you what they wanted you to see; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not precisely. They brought us to the place where it has happened that -- it was easier to found so -- they want to show us what we should see as they did, they brought us at the spot where it has happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So as you just said, they wanted to show you what you should see, right?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, when you went up there --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, I'm not sure that's what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It's on line 13 going into line 14, he said they want to show us what we should see.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I think he said on line 12, "They brought us to the place where it has happened."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. It's clear that the witness had some hesitation to follow the suggestion made by Mr. Kehoe to him which was suggestive to the aspect of just to see what they wanted to he show you or at least bring you to the place where it happened. It's all a rather semantic issue. It's clear that something had happened and that they escorted you to that place not blindfolding you on the way there, not -- so therefore let's continue, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The matter is clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Sir, when you got there -- when you were there is when the shelling took place. When you were there, sir, did you see any type of -- well, let me withdraw that question. On your way up there or at any time prior to that, did the ARSK inform you or any of the other UNMOs that on July 30th, 1995, they were preparing an offensive in an around the Strmica area against the HV, did they tell you that?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, at least they didn't tell me. Maybe some other UNMO, but I think when that would have happened, I -- our team would have heard it also.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me turn to D338. If we could go to the top of the page of D338 which is the 30th. This is the diary of Captain Berikoff. On the 30th of July is the day that you went there; correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: "Up at 0700. Another day. Not sure what will happen today. It was quiet last night. Everything happened today. Got tasked to go and spend the night in Strmica with the Kenyans. Very interesting, saw all kinds of equipment on the way there. BMPs, M-12 anti-tank gun, M-84 tanks and everything. Shelling started about 1830 and continued for about 1 1/2 hours. Two M-84 tanks crossed border of BH, Bosnia-Herzegovina. Then one came back a couple of hours later. Many ARSK around the area." Excuse me, 11 and a half, that's an hour and a half, I apologise. Did you see any of this equipment in the Strmica area that was observed by Captain Berikoff during this time? On the same day?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't see it on 30th of July because even I -- as I told yesterday, we didn't have -- we didn't go into Strmica because we were shelled and then we turned back.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, sir, you is say that you were shelled. There was shelling. You don't know what the target of that shelling was, do you?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, but it was very close to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, I mean let me go back to your diary, sir. And if you can point to your diary of the 30th of July with the Court's permission. If I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If counsel is looking for D224, that's the excerpt from the 30th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I have that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Reading this, sir, of the 30th of July, you noted, and I have to pull it from one of your statements, you noted that in this particular location, that there was a checkpoint nearby, was there not? Was there a checkpoint nearby where the shelling came in?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The checkpoint was -- I don't remember the distance exactly but as I told yesterday, we were stopped before Strmica and the checkpoint was somewhere inside Strmica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, the checkpoint that was in Strmica, how far away from it was where you were stopped?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe 300 to 500 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, in that area as you go into Strmica, and if we can go to -- if we can go into private session, briefly, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We turn it to private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Marti, at any time during this particular ride back and forth, and now I'm talking about the ride back with the liaison officer, did the liaison officer ever tell you that the ARSK, on the 30th of July, was engaging in troop movements up from Knin through Strmica to go to the confrontation line outside of Grahovo?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, this particular visit with the liaison officer that he was going to show you, he was going to show you this shelling to attempt to get pressure by the UN on the HV to stop shelling the Strmica-Grahovo road, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: For us, it seems like there was the normal procedure, there was shelling then they have contact with the liaison officer, then we go on the field and make the crater analysis. So for us it didn't look as this special event should have had special intention.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let's just stay with that for one moment. The shelling was -- you were called upon to do the shelling analysis by the ARSK, were you not?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's where the ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And correct me if I am wrong, but the reason why the ARSK wanted the UN to examine the shelling was to put pressure on the HV to stop shelling the Strmica area; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, this question has been asked. This question has been answered almost literally using the same words where the witness explained that it was, for him, it looked to be the normal procedure and nothing special, and he didn't know anything about it, that's what he told you. If you look at page 15, line 16, 17, 18, and 19, then you see that it's almost literally the same. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I understand, Judge. If I can have just one moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let us move to another issue, sir. You talked a little bit yesterday about the shelling of the Cetina area; do you recall that, sir?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, the -- if we can go to a particular item, and if we can go to D219. If we can just blow up the centre of -- yeah, to the left-hand side, yeah. Now, does that area look familiar to you, sir?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay. Knin being the -- over to the left-hand side, if you can just pull that up just a little bit. If we can just move it up a little bit, Mr. Usher, up. Can you just scroll up. Scroll down, I guess, is the right word. Down a little bit more. Down more. Just down to the -- more just down a bit more. Stop right there, please. Now, sir, this is a working map for the July 1995 area and the area we have depicted here is the Cetina valley area, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean the map is very unclear but when you say it, it must be.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, let's turn to -- you understand -- you see the lake down here. Are you familiar with that area?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Are you familiar with Vrlika area near -- just nearby the lake?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let's just go to a -- before we go to this, you are aware that the town of Vrlika was the headquarters of the ARSK 1st Light Infantry Brigade, were you not?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was aware that there was an HQ, but I don't remember, as you said, which brigade or battalion or whatever.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did the -- in addition to a brigade headquarters, did the 7th Dalmatian Corps have a forward command post in Vrlika?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have not seen a special command post. What I saw in Vrlika was the office or the HQ of 1st Class Captain Popovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You are familiar that Knin was the headquarters of the 7th Dalmatian Corps is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did you know in Vrlika in addition to having a headquarters for the 1st Light Infantry Brigade that there was also a forward command post for the 7th Dalmatian Corps?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Just to make clear what the witness said is at line 17 that he was aware that there was an HQ, but he didn't remember whether it was a brigade or battalion or whatever and counsel keeps naming units. That might be in evidence but that's not what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi, let me just have a look. I think Mr. Kehoe asked for headquarters and a forward command post, two different things. As far as the headquarters are concerned, the witness testified that he was aware of the existence of a headquarters but not what unit it exactly was and then the forward command post, he was then asked about that again in relation to what existed in Knin and that's a different area. It's not exactly the same as the previous questions. Please proceed, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We can turn our attention --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Before I leave this map, Mr. Marti, how far away from the lines of confrontation, approximately, was the Cetina valley?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't see it on the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Just from your recollection, just an estimate, how far away was it?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Without having a look at my map, I just can guess, five, six kilometres maybe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Approximately 5 or 6 kilometres?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe even more because the map we were using normally was scale 1 to 100.000 so it's not so easy.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, when you had come in June of 1995 and early part of July 1995, the HV had just engaged in a series of successful offensives up the Dinara into the Livno valley; isn't that right? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me turn your attention to your diary at -- on the 4th of July and on the 4th of July in your meeting with Captain Popovic, he wanted the UN to put more personnel up on the Dinara, didn't he? With Your Honour's permission if he could just refresh his recollection from his diary.

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to my diary on the 4th of July --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, the third of July, I take it back, the 3rd of July, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was the 3rd of July when we had a meeting in Vrlika with Popovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: He notes and the translation notes, "In summary he demanded more peacekeepers in the Dinara Mountains as quickly as possible."

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: "Because otherwise Split, Sibenik, Zadar, and Dubrovnik would be bombarded so that the same thing did not happen to Krajina as happened to Western Slavonia." He, at that point, Mr. Marti, was very concerned about the successful offensives that had been conducted by the HV, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: He didn't call us that was an official offensive by the HV. By the way, that area was part of the UN protected zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Can you explain to me why Julia was sweating while interpreting. You note that Julia broke into a cold sweat while interpreting. What was that about?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The interpreter, she was very nervous to be together with a commander from so-called her side because she wanted to do the job very well and it was a first time for her that she was as an interpreter inside a meeting with important or high ranking persons from her side.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me turn you to another map, if I may. Yes. If I may, I'd like you to take a look at 1D30-0005. The area that we have highlighted in red, Mr. Marti, is the area of the 1st Light Infantry Brigade. Are you familiar with the three battalions that were in the 1st Light Infantry Brigade?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I am not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: In this particular area, did you know whether the 7th Corps had howitzers assigned to the area of the 1st Light Infantry Brigade?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Based on your military experience, are you familiar with the fact that there is artillery that is assigned on a corps level, artillery that is assigned on a brigade level, and artillery assigned on a battalion level?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Based on your testimony, you are unfamiliar of the artillery that was assigned on the corps level; right?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, on the brigade level at this level, are you familiar with the howitzers and T-88 or T-76s that had been assigned to the 1st Light Infantry Brigade at that level?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I am not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And I take it that you are unfamiliar with their deployment of artillery on a battalion or on a company level?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That area, I'm not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So are you familiar with how the 1st Light Infantry Brigade deployed their troops in these three battalions?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No audible response]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The answer does not appear on the transcript. I think you said you didn't.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't know anything about these artillery systems in these regions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But the last question was about the deployment of troops. Are you familiar with how the 1st Light Infantry Brigade deployed their troops in these three battalions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I was not familiar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, you noted for us yesterday that, if I may, and this is on page 4590 line 16 through 18, you said, "We didn't see any military target or military troops or what could have been a target to be shelled by a grenade." Now, sir, an individual testified, Captain Jeff Hill testified that he was in the Strmica -- excuse me, the Cetina valley at the end of July and I'm dealing with 3808 going into 3809. And he observed T-54s, T-72s, APCs, and MP2s as well as 130 metre towed artillery, and I will give you the actual page reference for this but to be specific, it's 3809 lines 12 and 13. Now, you didn't observe that weaponry, did you?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mentioned yesterday when at that very day, Sunday 9th of July I made crater analysis in this small hamlet near Cetina and by that time, what was I observed was that the house was hit by an artillery grenade, that the people are complaining and what I also observed that around the house and in the near neighbourhood, there was no military target. That this was what I observed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Sir, you cannot tell us -- I'm sorry. Sir, you can't tell us whether or not a tank was rolling past there at the time, can you?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That very day, I didn't see any tank.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No, no. The day that the shell was fired and you were not there, you can't tell us whether or not a tank was rolling past and that shell was aimed a at a tank, can you?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because I came after the shell.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, are these not facts of common knowledge?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If I'm not in Amsterdam and if a shell falls yesterday if I was not there, of course there is always the theoretical possibility that someone reported to me that there was a shell driving there, but it's --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may. The obvious implication by the evidence that has been led by the Prosecution is that the HV was firing on a civilian target and using this witness and others to demonstrate that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's the obvious implication and not necessarily for this Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And Your Honour, I'm just trying to meet their evidence in the sense that this -- the army had --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, I do see your point, but you can draw our attention to that fact without putting questions which are obviously also -- we know the answer in advance and think until something very special happens.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm always encouraged by your conclusions, often times trying to meet the Prosecution's evidence, I try to go through the paces so we can get there. I certainly don't want to spend any more time on it than I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, with regard to the harvesting of this particular area, the fact is that General Gotovina ordered that there should be no more shelling to allow the Serbs to harvest; isn't that so? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I -- I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me show you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's ask the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Whenever during my mission, I have never heard the name Gotovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, have you any knowledge on the subject of how Mr. Gotovina dealt with complaints about farmers when harvesting apparently were reported to be shelled. Did you have any knowledge of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You do know, sir, that the harvesting went through. That the harvesting took place.

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The harvest took place, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I can offer this map on the 1st Light Infantry Brigade into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: It would be useful if we could be given the underlying information.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honour. The underlying information is seized ARSK documents which we will gladly share with the Prosecutor that lays out the -- or delineates the area of responsibility of the 1st Light Infantry Brigade as well as the units that are under that both at the battalion and the infantry level -- company level, excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: On its face we don't have an objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's then do the following: You will meet Mr. Kehoe, who will explain to you the further basis on this map and you have an opportunity to revisit the decision of the Chamber within the next 48 hours. I take it there will be sufficient time for such a meeting or exchange of information at least.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit D388.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D388, with the proviso as I just expressed is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Marti, we're going to shift gears and we're going to move to the 4th of August and talking about the shelling of Knin. Your diary reflects that you were in -- and you also testified that you were in Podkonje at the time?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: At the shelling. And you likewise went to the basement of your neighbour by the name of Milan; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And during the course of that day, you were sitting in Milan's cafe, and I'm referring to your 2007 statement -- excuse me, I'm referring to your diary of the 4th, that you sat in Milan's cafe most of the day and followed the activities on the news.

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not in Milan's cafe, it was just his normal house. It was not a special cafe. It was his private compound.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, I mean if you can turn to your diary for the 4th of August. You note, if we can, we follow the news in Milan's cafe eat goat meat and very dry meat it is, salad, bread, and have beer. Is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, but it was not a special, a public coffee shop, I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: But basically you and the other folks in Podkonje just sat out the actual shelling of Knin?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: We saw that there was shellings of Knin and in the morning, the first electricity went off and after a while, also our walkie-talkies run out of electricity so after a while, around lunch, we didn't have any connection with our HQ in Knin and we didn't have any information anymore what's going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You told us yesterday at page 4634, line 5, "I mean we couldn't see directly from Podkonje to Knin because there was a small hill in between." So you didn't actually see what was being hit during the shelling, did you?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it was impossible to is see from Podkonje directly on Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, you then, according to your diary, had dinner at 1830; is that right, sir? I think it's the same paragraph you note that in the evening, family of Biljana Dobricevic invites us for -- over for sour-crout, meat, bread and rakija?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Around 1930.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, 1930. Now, sir, now this is now about 7.30 in the evening, but it's actually before that because you said 1930 after about an hour. Now, at 1930, at about 7.30 in the evening you note that at that time, at 7.30, is when people went into a panic and I note your P415, paragraph 3, this is page 2 -- page 2 of statement, paragraph 3. "All of a sudden, the whole village was in a panic." Now, this, sir, was after Biljana came down to say that the HV was going to come into the area; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not a panic started and during that panic situation, Biljana came to me and asked for fuel for her cars but it was like -- you know before -- we didn't know what actually is going on. I even remember the people tried to make the mattress ready in the cellar for the children. Nobody was, I mean in my opinion, by that time in this hamlet, Podkonje, nobody was expecting the attack from the HV army but then all of a sudden, it was like somebody has turned a switch. For me, it was amazing like before there was quiet procedure with drinking, eating, I mean we didn't know what's going on but then all of a sudden, something must have happened. They must have got some information or whatever but it was a real full panic. I mean they were very scared and I remember Biljana shouted on me, "Oh, once more, UN cannot help us." Then I tried to, as I have described it, I managed to get fuel for her cars, and we get possibility to went into the Knin HQ of UN.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, that panic came, according to your diary, at approximately 7.30 at night; right?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, let me show you D137. If we can go just on D137. Now, sir, this is an evacuation order signed by Milan Martic at 1645 hours to evacuate and of course this order is before the 1930 panic that you witnessed. Now, just carrying on, Biljana's both father and brother-in-law were in the militia weren't they?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. I cannot confirm that because I didn't have so much contact only contact I had with Biljana was because she was only one in this hamlet who was able to speak English. But I don't know anything about her brother and her father or whatever they did or whatever they were doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Turned to P416, page 14. This is your 1997 statement. Do you have that, sir? P416, your 1997 statement, page 14. Line 30, the father himself was a militia member in the vicinity of Strmica. Line 33, the husband and the daughter were -- the husband of the daughter was in the militia.

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no that are not the same people. These are the people who was rent our -- the accommodation in Podkonje, but not the brother and father of Biljana who was in the hamlet in Podkonje.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I understand. Thank you for the clarification. It's not clear from your 1997 statement but in any event, these two individuals, you were going to get fuel for them for this family to leave; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Podkonje.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Right?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: But these are not the people mentioned here. Here are the people who are mentioned who has rented the houses in -- they had two houses, one in Knin and one in Podkonje and they have rent the house in Podkonje to the UNMOs but that has nothing to do with the family of Biljana which -- whom I helped to get fuel for evacuation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, these two individuals that you rented from that were the father and the brother-in-law that were in the militia --

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: In -- mentioned here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes. Those are the ones you got fuel for; correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Who did you get fuel for?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I got fuel for the people -- for the neighbours people in Podkonje. You know, there was a small hamlet and in one house, the UNMOs lived and around these houses were some other family. One was the family of Milan, and one was the family of Biljana. But these families actually has nothing to do with the family who rent our house because that family was established in Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I got the fuel for the family neighbouring family in Podkonje not for our landlord's family.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, if you turn to page 15 of this document, and you go to line 2. And you say, "She even over looked at her father forehandedly stowed two jerry cans of petrol in the car." Who was that?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the family in Knin in -- who managed to escape to Belgrade because this family by the way I'm still in contact today, that was our landlord's family and the father was in the militia so the father was not with the family together but that's what they told me after when I met the family, I managed to find the family when they have escaped in March 1996 in Belgrade; and they told me what has happened to their family, so when the shelling started in the morning, the daughter was too nervous to drive the car, even her father have prepared the car for evacuation but he she couldn't manage to start the car. But that has nothing to do with the situation how it was in Podkonje by that -- on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Just going back to what you just said, the father did prepare this car for evacuation, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but that was in Knin, not in Podkonje.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And as part of this evacuation, you also told -- one of the women told you that she got on a bus to leave the area as well; do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: But that was from the family in Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not the people in Podkonje.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So buses were organised to evacuate the population?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if that was an organised bus or whatever.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: But she told you that she took a bus?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, you also note that on line 6 of page 15, that, "Chance brought it about that both mother and daughter met both husband and son-in-law, the young husband of the daughter in Banja Luka."

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, that is what he they told me in March in Belgrade. They were met themselves together in Banja Luka, just by the accident.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Was it by accident that they met or was it by accident that they went to Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was -- as they told me, it was by accident that they met in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yeah. But you realise that the plan of the RSK was to go to Banja Luka, do you not?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that that was a plan of the RSK to go to Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me show you D182, just very briefly. If we can just blow up the centre of "the RSK authorities." This notes, sir, this is although the date is wrong, it's the 4th of August, we all agree, and this sets out on the 4th of August that the actual plan was to go to Banja Luka. You are not a ware of that?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let's shift subjects if we can and go to the actual shelling itself. And you noted for us again on page 4634 that you didn't see most of the shelling. And in your 2007 statement, on page 35, and if I can get the right date for this, this is paragraph -- paragraph 35 which is page 6. You noted for us that when you were on your way -- page 6 of the top paragraph on paragraph 35, that when you were on your way to the UN compound the evening of the 4th, you didn't remember any shelling at that time; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was right but I mean you have also to understand the situation in which we were. I mean we tried to have evacuate ourself and there was really a big panic and I -- even when I -- even if there would have been some shelling again, I mean you could -- you don't hear it but what I remember was another shelling is Saturday morning on the 5th of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, with regard to the actual destruction of Knin and caused by the shelling, you noted for us on P415 in the fifth paragraph, second from the bottom on page two, "My area of responsibility was outside Knin so I can't give you any exact statements about the destruction of the city." That's right, isn't it? Do you want to review your statement, sir, it's P415?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So you can't give us any statements about the destruction, right?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, you noted yesterday during the course of your testimony about the actual targeting and -- this is a reference back to your prior testimony, I do believe that Mr. Waespi read. Paragraph 10, page 17 of Exhibit 417. When you were talking about the shelling of Knin, you note that, "There was no military target. The only thing which might have been there was a camp close to the UN camp. A place where a few tanks and a repair depot were located but it was so close to the UN camp that its targeting would have been useless." Do you recall saying?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, the premise that you have about the shelling of Knin being a violation of the law is based on your conclusion that there was no military targets in Knin other than the base that was next to the UN; is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me -- I'm sorry. Let me turn our attention to 1D17-0201. This is, Mr. Marti, an ARSK intelligence department General Staff report signed by a Colonel Mihajlo Knezevic, and I asked you to take a look at -- if we can blow up that fourth paragraph. It notes: "Knin was attacked by Livanjsko Polje from several directions and by the time this information was drafted between 200 and 300 rounds of different calibres impacted on the town. The first strike was carried out on the building of the SVK General Staff." Now, that's a military target, isn't it, Mr. Marti?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, the witness has told us that he was not aware, when he made his assessment of military targets. Of course the Chamber has received evidence which at least strongly suggests that there were quite a number of military targets. Now, to go through all of them and then ask the witness whether he would consider that a military target, where his assessment apparently is based on the assumption that there is no military targets is not of great use.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I understand, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are not seeking the judgement and we are not here to educate the witness, but we are here to hear what he can tell us and then of course we will evaluate any flaws or any strong points in it. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The rest of this paragraph and then I'll offer it, Your Honour. Which -- I'll just offer this document into evidence, Your Honour. 1D17-0201.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D389, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D389 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And just going into the provisional assessment. In your 2007 statement, you said you were unaware of the provisional assessment that was signed by Mr. Hjertnes, is that right, concerning the shelling of Knin? I turn your attention to your 2007 statement 417.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: That's paragraph 59.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. 59.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: On paragraph 59 of your 2007 statement, you note that you were --

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have been shown a report ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: But you hadn't seen it prior to that? I note that you were on leave between the 14th and the 22nd?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see these paper before.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: During this time, when Colonel Hjertnes come back, did he express to you at any point that he had concluded that people who had lived through the shelling in Knin on the 4th and 5th had a difficult time objectively analysing the shelling? Did he ever tell you that?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It was a fact that the people that were there during the time were given CTO leave; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean who -- who?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The UNMOs that were present in the Knin area on the 4th and 5th were given compensatory time off, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, but that was one day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay. Were others given --

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean in my team, that was one day when we were allowed to go to Sibenik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Were others given more time off?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: But you yourself were gone front 14th to the 22nd?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, but that was the normal leave in the posting. I mean after -- the normal procedure was that you have to stay 30 days on the job and then you have five days off. And because I was -- I'm still living in Switzerland, I have in these five days, I could manage to go home but normally, some other UNMOs like from Russia, Bangladesh, et cetera, they just spend their leave in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, sir, you noted that you had not seen the provisional assessment. Had you seen an assessment by CIVPOL which basically said the same thing as the provisional assessment that this shelling was directed towards military targets? Did you see that?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me continue on to another subject, sir. This has to do with your comment again, I believe Mr. Waespi read on 417, page 17 paragraph 110 at the bottom of that page, talking about the withdrawal of the Serbs, you note on the fifth line from the bottom of that paragraph, "And they also fired on the refugees." Now, you never saw the HV firing on refugees, did you?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because during the Operation Storm, we were not allowed to leave the UN camp in Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, sir, were you familiar with the fact that as the Serbs were withdrawing, they were firing back on the advancing HV?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, let me read you a statement -- by the way you, are you familiar with the concept of fighting withdrawal?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but not mixed with refugees.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, if the Serb -- if the RSK was in this refugee column and firing back at the HV, that would be a fighting withdrawal, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Hmm, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: This is a -- this statement of Mr. Hill on page 3854, line 17: "Captain, you noted for us that as you went up these roads, you saw and followed the path of the Serbs who evacuated. You saw tanks and other items, right? Answer: "Yes." Question: "And when you, and I don't have the transcript but then you mentioned something about fighting and moving." Answer "Yes." Question: "Can you just explain that manoeuvre just a bit." Answer: "Starting at the intersection with Otric, there was a huge ammunition dump for lack of a better item in a field crates six or seven feet high." Going down to line 7 on 3855: "So it appears as if the Serbs as they were going back, they were falling on to the ammunition using the ammunition to fire, to fight and to continue back as the Croats were pushing them." Question: "And now you likewise observed tanks, Serb tanks and that had been abandoned and then were then pointed back on the road." Answer: "Yes." Question: "Did that indicate to you that they were fighting oncoming troops?" Answer: "Their muzzles were" -- sorry, "their muzzles were pointed towards the Serbs were advancing." Correction -- Judge Orie intervenes with a correction and the witness says, "the muzzles of the Serb tanks were pointed back down in the direction the Croats were advancing." Now, that type of fighting withdrawal was consistent with what you observed on the road as you came up the road from Otric going north, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I have no observation on the road from up -- from Otric up going north. What I mentioned was on the street leaving Knin, after the Operation Oluja when we were allowed to go on patrol again, I saw on one side, I saw on the one hand, I saw craters in the street, artillery craters. And what I saw on the street side were civilian cars which were no more able to move that were civilian clothes, furnitures and also dead animals. That is what I stated. But I didn't saw tanks or howitzer or whatever. That was my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And with regard to the craters, you don't know when those were fired or who fired them, do you?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: At least they were -- the craters were not on the street before Operation Oluja.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: During Operation Oluja, you don't know who fired them?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask one question in this respect. When looking at the craters, could you determine whether the fire was from south to north or from north to south on the basis of the shape of the impact? Did you pay any attention to that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, we didn't pay much attention on that because we didn't make special crater analysis from these craters on the street. We just saw that there were artillery impacts on the street. But we didn't analyse it from which direction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: A crater analysis requires quite a lot of things and so you didn't even in a very limited way analyse the craters so as to -- okay, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now if we can just shift subjects if we can to the writing on the house of -- this is a Croatian house?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, it's 10.30 and you are entering a new subject. I suggest that we first is have a break. Before we have a break, I would like to ask Mr. Usher, we'll have a break for approximately a half an hour, Mr. Marti. Could you please follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As far as time is concerned, Mr. Kehoe, could you give us an indication?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I will finish, Your Honour, no later than the end of the next session and possibly before that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I could estimate one hour of cross-examination, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Cayley.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: We have no questions for this witness, Your Honour, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That means that we'll be able to conclude the testimony of this witness today unless, Mr. Waespi, you will have long re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I don't anticipate that, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So far, ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll have a break and we resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Marti, in your 1997 statement, P416 at page 10, line 18 and 19, you noted that your neighbour wrote "Croatian house" with big letters on the house. Do you recall that, sir?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And who was this person who did this?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was a Croatian female who came back from I don't know where and she overtook this house, it was just on the back yard of the house where we were living and she wrote "Croatian house" on it, just to be sure not to be looted or attacked also.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Was she an older lady, younger lady?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: She was quite young, about 30 years.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: But a civilian?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Civilian, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And you noted for us in the same page at line 16, that writing "Croatian house" was not always a guarantee that the house would remain untouched. Was that your experience?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it happened that even houses were touched or partly damaged which at the signal before Croatian property or whatever.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Sometimes it just didn't make a difference?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me just show you P123?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps when it's shown on the screen, Mr. Kehoe, could the witness explain what he exactly meant by "she overtook this house."

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That would be on line 19 and 20, Mr. Marti.

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That means the house was abandoned after Operation Oluja, and she came and just came in and thought that was her former property or the property of some relatives of her or something like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is so with a claim that the property belonged to relatives for her she took after the house was abandoned.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Had she been a refugee prior to Oluja?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay. Let me show you P123. That is sitrep of August 19th, 1995. And Mr. Usher, if we could go in -- bear with me one moment, I'll get you the exact page. About four pages in, please to the E. That's it. And under the E, the second paragraph -- this is a sitrep from 19 August at Biocic the UNMO patrol met an old whom who normally is living in Sibenik. She asked them to write a message saying, "This is a Croatian house but I am living in Sibenik so please do not burn this house." Were you aware of this event, Mr. Marti?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in details but in similar events as well that people came back or said they have been living before here so that these are property or they told us we are now coming back and take over our former property.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And were you aware of this woman asking UNMOs to write this --

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: About this still I'm not aware.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay. Now, let us turn our attention to the actual individuals committing these crimes and I note for your -- in your statement, your 1997 statement and again we are talking about P416, at page 12 and you're talking about looters in this instance. If we go to page 12, line 23. Are you with me, sir? Now, you note that the identity of these looters was always difficult. You have to speak into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We noticed that because it was not easy to see are they members of an army? I mean what defines a soldier? Is that he is carry a weapon or a gun? Or is it because he has -- he's wearing a uniform or parts of the uniform? So it was very difficult to identify these looters. Were they civilians or part of an army or whoever they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And you had that question in your mind through this period of time when you saw this looting; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let's just continue on with that part of the statement on the same page starting from line 23: "Trying to identify the looters was always difficult because first of all, the looters carried, or when they were in a group at least one of them carried a weapon, mostly an AK-47, and mostly they also wore parts of uniforms, either a combat jacket or combat trousers, at least one of them, they were young people, so whenever it was said that it must have been soldiers, one might has to differentiate. They belonged [sic] to a regular force or young people who did not walk around as soldiers of an existing unit but were just dressed like them." That was your experience in your questions, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me turn your attention to P154. And as this is coming up, Mr. Marti, this is a UNMO sitrep of 19 September 1995. If you can just scroll down the page, that page right there, before the 2 there, "Looting is still observed by soldiers and civilians." If you can move up four pages on the B, "And this is Team Sibenik reporting on that line," the last two lines, "The patrol observed men and civilian in uniforms looting the villages." If we can go to one last -- if we can just stay on that page, go on the page back. And -- in the Team Podkonje reported on the 19th, if we can roll up just a little bit there, scroll up that page. "Team Podkonje noted that it was assessed that the house was set on fire by neighbours returning to the area." One last item on this situation report is the next page. And I will ask you some questions about these after we review them, Mr. Marti. If we can just scroll down just a bit. And about midway through "But the remaining Serbs can observe looting of the remaining houses, the remaining Serbs states that the area earlier have been visited by HV soldier that behaved in a correct manner but they believe that the uniformed men visiting now are not real soldiers." So just taking these through, I mean part of the confusion, Mr. Marti, was that you had people in partial uniforms looting; right?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You had people in these partial uniforms and civilians looting; right?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And you were being told by some of the remaining Serbs that they didn't think that these were real soldiers.

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: As we see in the --

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So that led to a lot of confusion as to who exactly was responsible and how to identify these people; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, but it happened because there was no organisation who tried to establish at least a little bit of order. As I mentioned it yesterday to the not being, in my opinion, not so difficult to minimise the lootings over weeks and even months.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I understand, sir. But identifying the perpetrators based an all those factors was very difficult to do?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And then in addition to that, you have the civilians actually returning, the refugees returning; right? Is that right, yes?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And they brought with them, as you said yesterday, at page 4639, line 17, "I understood that there was also revenge." Some of those people that came back brought a revenge as well for what had happened to them; isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, that's so because they told us "Where the UN have been in 1991 when we have been pushed out? So we are just coming back to our places."

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: But some of these people as you noted on that same page, on page 4638 at line 8, "Of course when we also, we also tried to -- but what could we do against the looters? I mean when we were on the spot, with our UN vehicle they just disappeared." So when you came, these people left, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Normally they just disappeared on even sometimes, we get in contact with them, maybe we talk to them, and as I mentioned yesterday, already one example, someone told me oh, I'm just looking for a motor so here and some other told us as I mentioned before, where you have been some years earlier?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, in the midst of this, I think you noted that there was a lack of order and a lack of control and I refer back to your 1997 statement 416, page 8, line 9 and line 11. And you believe that there was some possibility to regain this control; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, this -- you also noted for us yesterday that the area was a very large area; right?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Do you know how large the size of the Krajina was?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have made a sketch very early in my diary just when I got into the mission and here I notice it was -- the area for our Team Podkonje before the Operation Oluja covered about 50 to 50 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, and that area is --

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: But that was prior to Operation Oluja. Even after Operation Oluja, there were more regions coming -- were added. As I mentioned before, before Operation Oluja, we didn't have access to all the places and after Oluja, we were able to go everywhere. So it was even much bigger than before.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: But the area that you were covering was vast, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And we had these people coming back as well as these other individuals looting and you simply couldn't cover all these areas, could you?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it was not possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, sir, did you know how many civilian police were available to the Croatian government to control this area?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And do you know how many military police were available?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how many were.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And the checkpoints he we talked about, you talked about setting up a checkpoint. Do you know how many checkpoints these civilian police and the military police is set up during this time?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I have seen was this checkpoint I mentioned yesterday near Plavno valley which was only manned a few days. Once I have seen the -- it was only not a real checkpoint, it was a two-man posting in Kistanje, and that's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So you don't know how many checkpoints they is set up?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, let's just talk about the checkpoint that you talked about yesterday. I mean the checkpoint was set up in the Plavno valley; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, where you come out -- where you leave the Plavno valley.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, when they set that checkpoint up, did the looting in those hamlets stop?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That I cannot confirm because I was not in Plavno valley when the checkpoint was manned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's what the witness, Mr. Kehoe, may I draw your attention to the fact that the last five, six, seven minutes, that approximately 70 per cent of your questions just repeat by reading what the witness said, reading what others said, asking the same questions that have been answered already before. And apparently, I mean that's at least how I analyse what you are doing is that you are seeking certain conclusions because from the remaining 20 or 30 per cent, I would say one-third is about what the witness doesn't know and that's all to demonstrate that his conclusions are wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Not that, Judge, with all due respect, Judge, it's some clarifications of his conclusions. During direct testimony, Your Honour, there was some very broad conclusions set forth by the witness and I'm just exploring the clarification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's take the last one, whether he saw these checkpoints. He answered those questions exactly yesterday that he didn't know how long they stayed because he was not present. It was in the beginning of the Plavno valley.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Judge, I had another question to follow up with that which is what I was setting up which was the next question following what Mr. Waespi brought up which is: Do you know the reasons why those individuals were taken off that particular checkpoint?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The only thing I say is that 70 to 80 per cent of what you did over the last five to six minutes and I checked it carefully was just repeating what was already said before reading to the witness, what others had said. This Chamber is interested in hearing from the witness what he knows rather than to hear again what he has said already before and what others have said before. So therefore, I have no problem if you ask him whether he knows the reasons of that. It is similar like spending a couple of minutes asking whether it takes you 20 or a 25 years in the Canadian army to have sufficiently gained experience to be a General and then the same for a Colonel and then -- I mean that's -- let's get to the point right away and let's ask the witness -- and I'm not seeking further comments. You may ask the questions to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, during this period of time, Mr. Marti, I mean were you aware of how many arrests had been made for lootings and burnings?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You noted during the course of your testimony at 4639, page 4639, line 2 when you were talking about controlling the area, you noted: "As I remember, on a map in the newspaper, there were five brigades who had been attacked Krajina so what did they do afterwards? Why didn't they provide more security?" Were you aware, sir, where those brigades went after Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Were you aware as an UNMO that the war continued against the Bosnian Serbs up on the border between Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That I was aware.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: But you are unaware that the brigades --

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You're unaware that the brigades --

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: -- that operate in the Krajina went there. Now, you noted also in your testimony that public statements could have been made with regard to this to cease the looting and any of the criminal activity in the area; right?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was my estimation that maybe that could have helped a little bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, you're talking about political leaders of the country making those statements, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't make that difference of any leaders political or military or whatever, just responsible people for that Krajina after Operation Oluja.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Do you know, sir, whether any Zagreb officials made public appeals to stop the looting and the burning?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, obviously one of the ways to stop crime is to investigate these matters. And I think what we talked about yesterday was P425 if we can bring that up. If we can go to the next page. This is the matter of Milan Marcetic and Suica Dusan -- Dusan Suica that we talked about yesterday, sir, and you mentioned some of your commentary about this.
