Across the bar table, Your Honour, I would like to offer an item into evidence which is 1D30-0017?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi, I don't yet know what it is but if you know --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It's a criminal report on this event.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D390.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D390 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, this notes it is filed on the 5th of October, 1995 on the two individuals that we just discussed. And it is a report of the MUP with an unidentified perpetrator where various steps for the examination took place. If I can offer this into evidence. Has it been admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It has already been admitted. At the same time, is there any way that we get this on the screen so at least we can have a glance at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Again, D390 is 1D30-0017. I'm delaying because I'm going to flip back to the other document, so I'm just giving Your Honour a chance to read through it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, I take it you are unaware of this filing, is that right, Mr. Marti? Did you know that a criminal report had been filed with the Ministry of the Interior?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we can go back to P425. And if we can just go up -- if I can just reference this for, Mr. Marti, can we just go to the next page. Because attached to this exhibit is a document noted HRAT activities. Can we go one page up, please. Now, the -- this note is HRAT activities. At the bottom of the page, without reading it, sir, it notes that the police arrived on the scene to take the bodies for autopsy. And at the bottom, the last two lines, it notes, "A few days after the event, Croatian police drove two of the villagers in order to help in the identification of three suspects, currently held in Zadar." If we go to the next page. The top of the page if we could blow those first two paragraphs up. "By the two witnesses, we were told that they could not identify the criminals among those three under arrest. However, they stressed even if they could identify the perpetrators they would not do so for fear of retaliations." "On the spot, we met four anti-terrorist policemen from Zadar. According to one of them, since the 30th of September, they have been instructed to patrol the area on a 24-hour basis. Also Croatian civilian police had received the same instructions and a patrol was encountered in the valley." Now, Mr. Marti, using this as an example, were you aware of this type of response by the Croatian police when such crimes occurred?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes I'm aware but it -- in some cases but not in all the cases so I hope there is not only one criminal report, there must be 184 according to our list of 184 dead bodies we found.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: But you were aware of this instance that --

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sometimes -- I mean we any case we had we tried to get in contact, special the team of Hussein Al-Alfi tried to get in contact with the authorities to clarify, but I mean the examples showed that in the case of Milan Marcetic, it was too late, he has been killed, and he thought he was safe according to his paper he had, as I mentioned yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I understand, sir. Let me turn your attention to another subject which had to do with your statistical numbers that you put together with Mr. Anttila and if I could turn to P176. And if we can go to the second page of this document. If we may, just looking at this for reference, Mr. Marti, this is a document that notes number of buildings totally damaged, partially damaged. And you come up with a final number at the last page of 17.270 buildings either totally or partially damaged. My first question for you, sir, is how many of these buildings were habitable?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean habitable.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: People could --

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say a correct number. Even -- I mean if a house is partly damaged, for example, you still can stay inside. It's not so comfortable, you mean we saw such situations. For example, one thing in one of my statements in my diary, I have noticed that we found an old woman in Plavno valley but you can look through her house. I mean the house was partly damaged she was still inside.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So looking at the partially damaged numbers that you have and in 176, you note that there are 9.207 of them, we can't tell from that how many of hose houses are habitable or not, can you?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not exactly. I mean to be precise, you have to look at each house before you make a assessment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And the idea of partially damaged would come into even if there was some gunshot fire on the front of that house, you would consider that to be partially damaged, wouldn't you? Even though it's habitable?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only say why I would have considered this house, but as you see, the list was covered together from different teams so I cannot say what was the general attitude how to consider the damages of the buildings.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well let us turn our attention to P68. Now, have you seen P68 before? And you're welcome to scroll through this, sir, it's a multi-paged document that is approximately -- not approximately, 70 pages long.

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have seen it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, this, sir, is a compilation of the team situation reports; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. That was made in the HQ sector in Knin. In the sector HQ in Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Was this the information that was used to compile the statistical items that you have set forth in 176? In other words, number of burned houses, partially damaged, damaged, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It can be a part of it. I mean the list that we were talking about before was put together from different informations we got every day from the different teams.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, if this is the information, the sitreps from the teams, what else did you have?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean who have what?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: What other information did you have that went into the compiling of Exhibit P76, the statistics of buildings damaged and partially damaged or totally damaged?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are no other informations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So all of the information that you used to compile Exhibit 176 should be set forth in these sitreps?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That also might be possible that some of the teams brought the information directly into the HQ, but I cannot be sure that any information was before exactly in a daily sitrep and information was only collected through the -- was condensed with all the sitreps. It might also be possible that some teams brought their information directly to the HQ.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: The question that was asked to the witness was, "So all of the information that you used to compile exhibit 176 should be set forth in these sitreps." I think it should be made clear or asked to the witness who compiled the information, Exhibit 176, what was the involvement of the witness --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Hold on a second. This is redirect examination and I don't want the Prosecution flagging answers to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you not talk at the same time. Let me just ... in order to better understand the testimony of the witness, it makes some sense to be better informed about how Exhibit 176 was compiled. That will certainly assist us in better understanding his answers. Mr. Waespi, perhaps you could introduce this suggestion in a different way so as not to give Mr. Kehoe the impression that you are starting redirect examination which I do understand was not your intention. Could you tell us a bit more about how this list on the basis of what and especially by whom this Exhibit 176 was compiled?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I will try it. This list which we were discussing before was produced by the team in -- the Human Rights Action Team in Knin. And as we know, Kari Anttila was part of it like me. And most of the computer work, it was Kari who typed the list. Me, I was not is so very used to use this computer system, it's the -- all these lines and et cetera. The basis of this information was on one side as I have mentioned already, was the daily sitreps, but I cannot say that there was no other information to collect -- no other information included as it might have been possible that they got direct information from other teams also. And I mentioned yesterday already also that when you saw the Team Podkonje we only mentioned the people that we found not the houses so I already mentioned already. Is so my main focus was not counting houses when I was on patrol, my main focus was always to care about the people who were still there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Was there any other -- I apologise. Other than the sitreps, to your knowledge, was there any other formal procedure within the UN UNMOs of collecting this information?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there was not a formal procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me -- if I might just have one moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me show you P65. Have you ever seen this form before, Mr. Marti?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, during the proofing, I have seen it. During the proofing time we were discussing it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, was this an official document that was used to collect information?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was a document that the Podkonje team used but it was self-made document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So this was a document that was only used for Team Podkonje?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if the other team -- or I don't remember if other teams had also the same form but that was only among us to make it easier when you were on patrol to figure out what he we had to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, looking at this form, what was to be included in this form as opposed to what was to be included in the sitreps?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That should normally also noticing in the sitrep.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So whatever is in these forms should also be in the sitreps?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I guess, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, when you were putting together P176, your statistical form -- well, let me withdraw that for one moment. You noted that this was a form for Team Podkonje. When you were putting your statistical information together to -- on P176 with Mr. Anttila, did you see dozens and dozens of these forms like this?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember that I have seen dozens and dozens of these forms.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You have?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that I haven't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You have not. Okay?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: For the benefit of the interpreters, the witness is kindly asked to speak up, if possible. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You heard that, Mr. Marti.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I heard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, just before we leave this area, on your definition of partially damaged and damaged, if we have a situation for instance if the police went in and broke in a door to do a search and the door was broken, would that be considered a partially damaged residence?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, if only a door is broken, that is not, in our opinion, that was not partially damaged.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let us turn our attention to the document that you -- came in previously but your name is on it, P177. Now, on the front page of P177, the document that you signed with Mr. Anttila, you have very specific percentages and numbers in the second paragraph, do you see that?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And of course those numbers are only as accurate as the underlying data; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let us turn our attention to 176 -- excuse me, P176, I apologise. Now, just looking at this report, with you noted yesterday that Team Podkonje didn't have the number of buildings that were in the villages because I think you told us that you were interested in people not buildings; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That, of course, throws the numbers off. But let us move away from, if we could, from Team Podkonje and move to the second to last page of this document. We were looking at the team Otocac numbers, I believe that's the -- a few pages up, if we can. Actually, five pages up. We're going to the second to last page in this document. The next page. It should be the Otocac number. Now, when you were compiling these statistics, Mr. Marti, did you notice that virtually all of the Otocac numbers were multiples of five barring a couple here and there? Firstly, all of these numbers on numbers of buildings totally damaged and partially damaged were numbers of five. For instance, if we look at Korenica: 3.000 buildings, 600 totally damaged, 24 partially damaged. Five down, Licki Osik: 2.000 buildings, 250 damaged, 550. When you were compiling these statistics, did you question this number gathering?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I mentioned already, I didn't compile these statistics myself, I think it was rather Kari Anttila than me. Maybe I would have also asked what is this -- all these numbers if possible dividing into five or ten. But I have maybe to explain a little bit this procedure of collecting information. Not all the teams had the same accurate or the same procedures. Some teams just drove through a village and they count the buildings and then they told us: Oh, we have been driving through this village. There are no people in this village. And I remember very well in one of the team leaders meeting where Steinar Hjertnes, I made an intervention because I told them, look, can you not just drive through a village. You have to calm down. You have to stop the car, you have to calm down, leave the car and you have to go around the buildings because when you come with a vehicle to a village, the first reaction to the people still living there is to hide because they didn't know who is coming so they hide. So to find the people you have to get out of the car but not all the teams did the same procedure as I did it in my team and so that's kind of maybe also be a case that they just figure out is numbers and it's not -- it must be -- or it cannot be very precise, even I can't imagine how is it that you count buildings in a village if you want to do it perfectly, you need at least half a day for each village if you want to do it in a proper way count the buildings, and then not only counting but also estimate what is the condition of the buildings, damaged, partly damaged or not damaged.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, let me go to this second page of this document just to -- not to leave Team Otocac alone, the second page in the Zadar Benkovac team. I think that's the same page. If we go to the next page. If we look at the numbers from the Zadar-Benkovac virtually all of those barring an individual one, those are all multiples of five as well. So these numbers themselves are not accurate numbers where -- not precise numbers are they?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, when you were going through here, you didn't account for the fact that, for instance, Rodaljice, you see that in there, you have 701 buildings, 118 partially damaged, 230 fully damaged, you didn't account for the fact that that's a Croat village?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I didn't ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, this particular item, these items of evidence, and -- you were doing this in conjunction with the Human Rights Action Teams; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, when I was appointed as a Senior Liaison Officer this is Human Rights Action Team.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And the individual who was on the scene at the time was an individual by the name of Edward Flynn, E. J. Flynn; do you remember him?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember Flynn.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And just looking at September, or his particular testimony on 11 April 2008, he was asked on page 313: "Did the UNMOs ever appear at the HRAT evening meeting and tell you that he had counted, let's say, 11.000 burned houses?" Answer: "No, not to my recollection." Question: "That number would have been something that you would have remembered; is that correct?" Answer: "I think so." Question: "Did they ever come back and say 16.000 houses?" Answer: "I know that the UNMOs were conducting a survey and I know that their numbers were high. Again as I say when I refer to my own estimate, my estimate is to be on the conservative side. I don't recall, though, any discussions with regard to those numbers while I was there." Now, just one last inter -- delineation there. Question: "Let's discuss, then, what would you discuss at the HRAT meetings at which UNMOs are present and if they counted 11.000 homes, would that be something that you would have discussed at the evening meeting of HRAT?" Answer: "Yes." Question: "Is so you're telling us at least through your time which I believe you said was 16 September, no UNMO came to a meeting and said we've counted 11.000 burned houses?" Answer: "I only recall and I only reported on the sightings that had been made and yeah, I don't recall at that we discussed any information you described." Now, can you explain to me, sir, why this type of information with these numbers would have been considered or -- let me withdraw that, would not have been discussed with the person who was in charge of these HRAT teams. Do you know?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot anything explain what this Mr. Flynn is telling here because I don't know him. I have never met him. But I have attended several meetings together with Hussein Al-Alfi together with UNHCR, together with Red Cross, so I was in different meetings, but I don't know this Mr. Flynn.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So you can't explain why he thinks --

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: -- your numbers are high?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me turn your attention to P169.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, may I take it that you wanted to ask the witness whether he can explain why Mr. Flynn thought the numbers --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- the numbers to be high. There is a difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let's turn to P169.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: This is a sitrep of 20 October 1995 and if we can turn in three pages. I want to ask you if you were a -- at the bottom of that page, "Other significant incidents." If we can just blow that up just a bit. Now, in this, this is quoting a Slobodna Dalmacija, by the way this is an UNMO sitrep, a Slobodan Dalmacija article where it quotes General Cermak noting about the burned and destroyed homes: "We have been told to the ambassadors that information proclaimed by UNCRO of 22.000 burned and destroyed houses in the former Sector South, in other words, 70 per cent of all the objects in the area is completely untrue. According to our reports there is a number of 2.000 to 3.000 houses, not 22.000, General Cermak said." Now, Mr. Marti, with the statistical analysis and the other problems with your statistics, the number that General Cermak assesses here is a more accurate assessment of the actual damage to the houses in the former Sector South, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That I cannot say because I don't know what General Cermak was -- the basis of his assessment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me just ask you one last area, sir, and it has to do with on the freedom of movement issues. In your 1997 statement on page 4, line 25 to 27, it says, "On one day Lieutenant-Colonel Steinar Hjertnes, the commander of Norwegian Lieutenant-Colonel, he was the sector chief told us to stop observing military movements or to rather concentrate on events in the humanitarian field." Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, in reality, you and the other UNMOs continued to monitor and report on military movements, didn't you? Yes?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No that's not true because after Operation Oluja our main task as a military observer that we had before, I mean it was over, there was no more UN zone of -- no UN zone of protection anymore so the main task to observe the cease-fire between these two parties was gone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: But we still noted when we military movement from the Croatian army but after a while Steinar told us hey, it's no more our job we don't have to observe what the Croatian army is doing because the situation has changed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, but the UNMOs continued to do it into October, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: To --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: To report on HV military movements, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, some of them -- that was like a normal procedure whenever you see somewhere some military activities, you note this down.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And this was outside their mandate, wasn't it as to what you were supposed to be doing?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, because the mandate was established for the mandate before -- for the situation before Operation Oluja.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, tell me in your -- tell me about Operation Black Crow?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Black what?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Black bird.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Black bird, black crow, I can point it to you in your diary of September 30th of 1995. Black Crow or Black Bird was an operation where all the UNMOs were tasked to go into Bosnia and Herzegovina and report on HV military movements and HV emplacements ; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So they went into an area contrary to the mandate that they had with the Republic of Croatia to gather information about UN military is; right -- HV military -- excuse me; right?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that we had after Operation Oluja what kind of mandate UN had with Croatian army.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let's just look at that, then, because it's in P28, the Akashi-Sarinic Agreement, if we can bring that up on the screen and you can take it look at it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there any need -- is it a primary focus to see whether the witness considers it contrary to the mandate or not or first of all to find out what actually happened?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, both.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, if we can just blow up the bottom of that and going into the next page, paragraphs 4 and 5 set forth what the UN was to do or not to do. Mr. Marti, are you familiar with this agreement?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Why don't we just -- if you can flip to the next page. Paragraphs 4 and 5, if we can read that -- if you can read that to yourself. Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now I have read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, when you told us in your statement of 1997, P416 on page 4 that Steinar Hjertnes said that the mandate had changed and that you were now supposed to -- that you had to stop observing military movements but rather concentrate on events in the humanitarian field, it's based on this agreement?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, Black Crow was -- Black Bird was ordered on the 30th of September, 1995. Who ordered that?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was Steinar. I mean I don't know -- sorry. I don't know if he has got some other order from somewhere, but he ordered it to the UNMOs to conduct these patrols.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And you knew, sir, that the UNMOs in Sector South were not supposed to be in Bosnia patrolling, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because I didn't know anything about the new agreement. The reason why we were told to do these patrols was because we had still a restriction of movement -- we never were able to drive over Strmica. I mean on the other side the direction south, Drnis et cetera, Maljkovo. We could go anywhere. The only road that which was closed for us after Operation Oluja was this road after Strmica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Sir, this monitoring of HV activities in Bosnia-Herzegovina was a change in your mandate -- excuse me, was counter to what you had been told by Steinar that you were now supposed to be involved in humanitarian endeavors; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, the task which we got which Operation Blue Bird was not to monitoring any military activities on the other side but to get to know what has happened according to the humanitarian side because we know there had also been fighting, et cetera, and our task was to monitor if there are still some people left, like left in Krajina, some people who wanted to run away or who couldn't run away, and I remember very well I was also on patrol in the Operation Blue Bird together with Bertil Svendsen and I remember this patrol very well because of two things once, the only person we found still alive in this region was an old woman in a hamlet, and this woman was a very bad conditions and the case too because I remember very well on the way back, Bertil and me realised we were driving through a minefield. So the task which we got from Steinar was not to monitor any HV movement but to get the picture of the humanitarian situation in these villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Marti, can you explain to me why this so-called Operation Black Bird or Black Crow is not contained in any of the sitreps that was produced by the any of the UNMOs during this time frame?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's mentioned in my diary.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You diary didn't get sent to Zagreb, did it?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Sir, prior to Operation Storm, you weren't authorised to patrol in Bosnia-Herzegovina, were you?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Prior to Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, the mandate was very clear inside the zone of protection, it said.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: When you went into Bosnia-Herzegovina for Operation Black Crow or Black Bird did you get the authorisation of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I mean I didn't get any as a UNMO in a patrol, any get any authorisation. What I got was the task from Steinar to go and we did it special places, I mean we had clear order where we have to drive, which road, et cetera, what we have to monitor and when we have to come back.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And you don't know if anybody else got that authorisation from the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, do you?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I might have one moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, about the date. I see the Chamber was not aware of any Black Crow, Blue Bird or Black Bird but apparently it started on the 30th of September.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was called Black Bird.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You used the word Blue Bird as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The colour of the bird was dark.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The indictment usually goes until the 30th of September which you -- I think you've drawn our attention to that, so apparently something happened and you think it was beyond the mandate. Where does the relevance --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: There has been tremendous amount of evidence that has transpired in this courtroom concerning restrictions of movement. We have had any number of witnesses coming in and telling the Court we couldn't go to this place or we couldn't go to that place all through August and September and frankly into October and the information inference why the HV or the Republic of Croatia of precluding such movement was because something bad was happening. Well, the answer to that is two scores. Number one, there was military operations, continuing military operations which clearly HV did not want the UN on and number two, there was activities such as this where they were going into areas that they weren't supposed to be, reporting back on HV movements contrary to the mandate. How does that come into play? We need only go back to the whole information that was transmitted by the UN to the ARSK or surreptitiously received by the ARSK during Operation Storm. And the restrictions of movement that place into those concerns by the HV and the Republic of Croatia concerning the activities of the UNMOs as they travelled around.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I see now how you perceive the relevance of your questions. Mr. Kehoe, could you tell us how much more time you'd need?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I might just have one -- just five seconds, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Five seconds from further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I know you will be very glad to hear this but I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I'm -- that doesn't make me happy as such.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Globally, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then Mr. Mikulicic, you are the next one but would it not be better to have a -- take a break a bit earlier then to resume at 25 minutes to 1.00 and if you could then conclude, even Mr. Kehoe managed to stay well within the time that he estimated. That you would then take 55 minutes, try to finish in 50 minutes, would 15 minutes then do for you, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I believe so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll take a break and resume at 25 minutes to 1.00 sharp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Marti, you will now be cross-examined by Mr. Mikulicic who is counsel for Mr. Markac. Please proceed, Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Marti, my name is Goran Mikulicic and I represent Mr. Markac in these proceedings. I'm going to ask a few questions although my learned colleague here already raised certain issues with you, and I'm not going to repeat them. I would appreciate to have your answers to the best of your recollection after so many years after the event. Mr. Marti, according to your statement, on the 12th of July, in 1995, you arrived in Zagreb where you underwent a week's training for UNMOs in the area of the so-called Republic of Serbian Krajina. Can you tell us briefly how did this training look like?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. First, I have to make a correction. I didn't arrive on the 12th of July but on the 12th of June in 1995 in Zagreb, 12th of June, 1995. I had a training as a UN Military Observer, a three-week training before in Switzerland. Switzerland organises every year a three-week training course for international officers from different countries for the teaching when you become a military observer, so actually the training so-called training week we had in Zagreb, that means every UNMO who came to the mission in Zagreb, he had to do some specific things, for example, the most important one for all of us was to get the driving licence as an UNMO, but there were also some few trainings in how to handle a car, how to repair a car, how to carry out crater analysis, how -- there were also some medical trainings but compared with the three-week training that I had before in Switzerland in spring 1994, this training was, in my opinion, only a how you say, a refresher training for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I understand. Within this training, were you given certain information about the historical and political situation pertaining to the area that you were going to be assigned to?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The information we got about the political situation was very few, I mean we got a situation how it was by that time, and we were told to attend every morning a briefing in the UNMO HQ in Zagreb, but this briefing, of course, was concentrated on the situation like it was by that time. So about historical situation, we didn't get so many informations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me if I say that in a certain way, you were learning as long as you went concerning these particular issues?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand the question well. You mean if we were learning by doing or what exactly is your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I will rephrase the question. In discharging your duties, on a daily basis, you actually became acquainted with the political situation in the area that you were intended to observe; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, but about the political situation, how it was in the field, we didn't discuss much. We just knew that we have to go to the Sector South and we knew the lucky one of us are posted on the Croatian side and less lucky one of us have to be posted on the Serbian side and then we have to try to manage and to do our task as well as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So on the 19th of June, you arrived in Knin as the head of the Podkonje Team, 7CW. How many vehicles did you have and how many men were there on your team?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not correct. I mean I arrived on the 19th of June in Knin, but of course not as a head of the team but as a simply a member. I mean I was the greenhorn in the team by that time. By that time, we had two vehicles for the team and due to security matters, every night, we had to park one of our vehicles in the UN -- in the sector HQ in Knin because we had only space, that means a garage, for one vehicle in -- on the team site in Podkonje.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: The territory that you were covering was pretty large, it stretched from Knin to Otric and then from Knin to the Bosnian-Herzegovinian border and on the other side, from Knin to Kistanje. With the vehicles and the men that you had, were you able to cover fully this territory in doing your daily job?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course it was a very difficult job to do with even when we had two patrols the whole day on the road, you cannot cover much because when you -- when you conduct a patrol, for example, from Knin to Otric, that means half a way, it's a half a day task, and the same when you travelled from Knin to Drnis and back with all the -- with the checkpoints that were there and et cetera, all the security measures we had to fulfill, so it was a very hard -- it was quite a difficult task to monitor the whole area quite properly. So whatever we monitored, by that time, it was only punctual monitoring, but we didn't cover the whole situation all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: After the Croatian authorities were restored in the territory of the so-called Republic of Serbian Krajina after Operation Oluja, you said that your mandate actually was altered. In that respect, did you receive any official instructions regulating the change of the mandate of UN monitors? In that context, I'm referring to official --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction -- to written instructions regarding the change of the mandate.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, as I have mentioned already before, we didn't or at least me, I didn't receive any written order that the mandate has changed to something else what we had before.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Concerning the subsequent change of the mandate, did you receive any additional training for your future tasks after the mandate was altered in this particular area?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we didn't receive any training because there was also no time. I mean the situation has -- had a change after Operation Oluja and the problem was that there were some people on the ground which were not safe so the time was running to do something for these people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you have an opportunity, Mr. Marti, to become acquainted with the organisation and the structure of the Croatian army, the civilian police, and, generally speaking, how the Croatian authorities operated in the territory that had been recently liberated?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't have this opportunity, what I only got was the punctual contact with some of the Croatian authorities in Knin and some of these contacts were quite difficult. I can give you an example. There was a graveyard near Knin and we noticed that there have been made fresh graves and on the graves was -- were putting crosses and on the crosses were not names but only NN and then numbers, but different numbers. I mean the numbers didn't follow 1, 2, 3, 4, for example, you have number 609 then 704 and so on and so on; and when I was in the team with Hussein Al-Alfi, we tried to find who is buried in this grave. We thought when there are crosses with different numbers, there must also be somewhere a list with different numbers. And it takes us days and weeks to figure out who was responsible for these graves, who had a list about these dead bodies who have been buried here. So during my time in Knin in the Human Rights Action Team, we were not able to find out who was buried there. Maybe, I don't know if after Hussein Al-Alfi or his -- somebody else finally managed to find out who had been buried there. So this is an example, I just want to show you how difficult it was to find somebody in Knin who was responsible, who was willing to help us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: In this context, were you familiar with the organisation and functioning of the civilian protection?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember one day, according to the case I have mentioned before, I had a contact with this -- what do you call -- civilian protection unit, but even they told us: We cannot help you. You have to address yourself to another organisation or another office in, I think it was Zadar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Marti, do you know what the role of the special police was in Operation Storm and after the Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you ever have an opportunity to talk to any member of the special police?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the only contact I had with the special police was together with this case in Podinarje where some Serb man wanted to come back from the forest and they wanted to be handed out to the Croatian authorities, but I think that was only a very small contact. By that time, I was in the team the first day when we wanted to go to Podinarje, we couldn't go because I think it was this -- what do you call the special police was carrying out an operation near the area of Podinarje and in the following time, I think we had a small contact with them, but that was the only one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you for this. We'll come back to this topic later. Mr. Marti, you mentioned that on the day when Operation Storm began, on the evening of that day, you were with the family of the neighbours where you were living and that at one point, panic broke out and you explained how it all happened. My question is: Were you aware how the media in Knin were informing the public? Were you able to follow the news that were disseminated through the Knin media?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not able. The only thing I noticed that during the day, also the radios went off because of lack of batteries so we were more or less cut off of any information in this hamlet, Podkonje.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you know that somebody from among the ranks of UNMO had an obligation to follow the work of the Krajina media and provide certain analysis, information, et cetera, in that respect?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Among the ranks of UNMO? I don't know. I have never heard that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: In your earlier testimony, you told us that you managed to provide and secure fuel for the vehicles owned by your neighbours. Allow me to read it out to you a portion of your statement which is Exhibit P415, which is your 1996 statement in which you say the following -- that's paragraph 3 on page 1, three lines before the end of the paragraph and I'm going to quote from your statement, [In English] "... from the UN headquarters in Knin but I have to they have to help us in return as long as we had Serbs with us, the Serbian soldiers wouldn't touch us." [Interpretation] Mr. Marti, can you explain why you needed protection so that you wouldn't be touched by the Serbs at that time in order not to prevent you in a certain way. What was this all about?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: You have to imagine the situation on that very evening. I mean we were still more or less hoped by the villagers, I mentioned before that in the morning in the -- UN send an APC to collect all the UN personnel in and around Knin but when this APC conducted by Jordanian military arrived near the village, they -- the villagers, they didn't let us go. So they said that people in the village, they said, "You have to stay. You have to protect us as a UN," so the APC drove back. But when, in the evening when the panic broke out, and Biljana asked for fuel and I told her first, look, and she shouted, "UN is not helping us." And even I had the discussion with the team leader, with the deputy team leader, the team leader was on leave, the deputy team leader was Felix Anglada from Spain and I had a discussion with him. I told him, we have to manage how that we be -- can get into a shelter. I mean the security for us was also important. So I made a deal with Biljana, and I was supported by Pavel Komper a colleague from the Czech Republic, so I told Biljana, look, I have no fuel here because our car is a Toyota Land Cruiser and this car needs diesel so we don't have any fuel for your car here, but I try to manage to get fuel for you but on the other side, you must guarantee that we, the UNMO team, can get safely into the UN compound in Knin. So Pavel and me and her and her brother drove in the private car from Podkonje to Knin and I went -- by that time, the road was messed up with refugees, et cetera, already, farmer trucks, et cetera, it was not so easy to get through this mess but when we arrived the gate, then Biljana's brother thought, ah, now you are safe but maybe you don't come because you are now in the camp. And then Pavel told them he will wait outside for me until I will come back with the fuel. I went inside the camp and of course it is not a problem to get two canisters of fuel. We went back, still through this whole mess, and now -- I mean now it was the key point of the situation because we had fulfill the part of our agreement, and now it was on Biljana's side to fulfill also her -- their part of the deal. And we had still this -- we had one car that Toyota Land Cruiser, so we packed as much as possible things in this car, and we were five UNMOs by that time, and drove back. But to drive back with a UN car during that mess, you needed a protection and the protection was one car of Biljana's family in front of us, then Biljana was sitting on my knees in the car, and behind us was another car of Biljana's family. And during the whole drive from Podkonje to the Knin HQ, I mean it was not so far, about 2 kilometres, the people were bumping on our car, they were shouting and I was very sure without Biljana and her family in our car and around our car, we would have never had the chance to get through this mess safely into the UN HQ.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Marti, for this exhaustive answer, but with all due respect, you did not answer my question. My question was: Why did you think that for as long as you had Serbs with you, the Serbian soldiers won't touch you? Why did you think that there was danger from the Serbian soldier for the UN vehicle and yourself as an UNMO?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, when you said the witness didn't answer your question. Your question was, the last part was: What was this all about? I wondered whether I would not have stopped the witness halfway because I didn't -- hardly could imagine that you would be interested in all these kind of details. Please take -- intervene when need be and do not wait for one page and then say to the witness he did not answer your question when he actually to some extent did. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I will follow your guidance.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Marti, let me repeat my question. I was referring to the following: Why did you emphasise that there was certain fear that you might be attacked by the is Serbian soldiers and I'm referring to your 1996 statement? We are talking about the Serbian soldiers.

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean the situation was very confusing and as we had some experience before, I mean there were -- have been -- I mean the situation was not so intense like in that very evening there had been -- have been different car hijacking so I mean when you are in a situation and everybody try to run away, I think it was very -- it could have happened very easily that they would have also tried to steal our car which we still had and then we would have been in Podkonje without any car. I mean together with this Serb family by that time was only a security measure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I understand. Does this mean that in the -- on the evening of the 4th of August when you went to Knin and back, between Podkonje and Knin, there was the is Serbian army deployed?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see any specific members of the army because I mean it was a crowd on the road and I didn't have time to look around. I was much more concentrated just what is in front of our car.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Very well. Let us move to another topic now. There was a lot of mention in your previous testimony of the looting that followed or the incidents of looting that followed in the aftermath of Operation Storm. You made several references to this, and I would just like to ask you a few questions with respect to this. In your statement given in 1997, that's Exhibit P416, page 4, line 11 to 15, you mention that in the area, there were some roving gangs who were committing looting in the area. Many of them were dressed in uniforms and that they were armed. Can you give us more details about these roving gangs and what did you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: We saw the -- as I have mentioned before, we saw groups or -- groups of young men who were roaming around and the people were afraid of them. And as I mentioned before, it was not easy to say that these are members of an army or civilians or whatever, but it had happened several times that we saw such groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And these groups associated you to roving gangs; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you can call it like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: On page 5 of the same statement, and I'd like to refer you to lines 5 to 9, you mention, and I will quote your statement, perhaps that's easier than have it interpreted: [In English] "The Croatian people came partly they as they told us, had been living there before. They came back, and they acted accordingly. When we confronted them that they would behave like looters, they told us that the same happened to them, and we also had a situation that we did not have enough translators and that we partly had to work with translators who were employed with the Croatian side ..." [Interpretation] Mr. Marti, have I -- am I interpreting this statement correctly when we speak of the Croats who had lived in the territory of the so-called Serbian Krajina and that when they returned to their own homes, they actually took things from deserted Serbian homes in order to be able to live a normal life, daily life at that time? Would you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I cannot fully agree because I said is only that some of the people who we talked with them told us that they come back, but they didn't say that they took anything from deserted Serbian homes because I just that -- this was my house before so I just come back to my house, but I didn't mention any details what they have took or if they have took something that have been property to the Serbian population before.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could we please have P68 on the screen, please? This is a summary of daily sitreps for the period between the 4th of September to 4th of October, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And while we wait for this to come up on the screens, I would like to show you the portion on page 861 which states the following: "On 12 September, an UNMO patrol in Mukinje ran into 6 men who lived in the village. Three of those men said that during the offensive, the first to come to the village were soldiers, Muslims, who looted everything." Do you have information about such instances, especially in the border regions between the Republic of Croatia and the Republic of Bosnia that civilians came from Bosnia across the border and looted the houses and villages in the area?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't have.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Alongside with soldiers?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: In these same documents, there is the following: "On the 9th, it was observed in Donji Lapac that soldiers bearing BH insignia were helping the refugees from Bihac and loading on to trucks with Bihac or Bosnia-Herzegovina plates to load cattle or other household appliances that were left behind by Krajina Serbs." Were you aware of the situation?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not in Donji Lapac. Of course I also meant sometimes that the looters tried to -- to steal the cattle and I remember one case when they tried to put a calf on the back of a Yugo car, I mean that looks very funny, and I'm sure the car needed a cleaning afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you for your reply. Mr. Marti, were you familiar with the evacuation plans put together by the authorities of the Republic of Serbian Krajina and their implementation? I would like to refer you here to the situation where you had columns of people leaving the area of the Republic of Serbian Krajina after the Operation Storm began?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not informed about the details about this plan. The only thing I was involved was when we had to collect these people, mainly in the Plavno valley and Podinarje area for the evacuation after Operation Storm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, in your last question, you link plans of evacuation and columns on roads you shouldn't mix that up in your question, of course you can ask the witness whether he knows anything about plans, we can ask him whether he has seen anything, we can even ask him or draw ourselves conclusions as to what he saw was consistent, what he knows about the plans, but try to keep matters clear and not to link matters where the witness might not -- here there was no risk or at least it didn't appear to be the case, but there's always a risk that witnesses are confused by these composite questions and then we'll have to ... Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you. [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could we have document 65 ter 005008 on the screens. This is a summary of daily situation reports between the 7th of the August up until the 8th of September 1995 which was in a certain sense authorised by Mr. Marti.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Authenticated - interpreter correction - by Mr. Marti.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Marti, in the upper portion of the document that we cannot see anymore, could the Registrar please scroll down a bit, in the upper portion of the document, we can see PM and circled and written by hand. Are these your initials?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You don't remember. To clarify this for the Trial Chamber, this is a document that is, I assume, identical to Exhibit P68 which was introduced with Witness Kari Anttila and signed by him. However, I refer to some portions of this document which are completely different both in the pagination and also in the paragraph numbering when compared to the document of Kari Anttila and in my future, I hope, brief questioning, I will use this document although there may be some confusion because they appear to be very similar but I am afraid that there are some differences because the pages do not correspond and we received this document as an annex to the document that the Prosecution used during the -- their direct examination. This is just for clarification purposes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, you earlier said that this document was in a certain sense authorised by Mr. Marti or authenticated. What was the basis for this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: The initials PM in the upper right-hand corner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I thought that was kind of an authorisation by the witness, Mr. Peter Marti.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So what you should have done is to refrain from telling what the case was and ask the witness which you did after that and then he said that he didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Didn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On page 118 of this document, I will quote a section, the first one which refers to evacuation: [In English] "At Sekanivrsak, we were informed that 71.200 refugees had used the checkpoint towards Banja Luka. Most of them had come from Knin. On the way to that checkpoint, UNMOs observed a lot of damaged trucks, cars, tractors and some goods abandoned along the road. Some cars were smashed by tanks. UNMO asked the commander if he had seen acts against civilians or RSK soldiers and were told this was not possible because all the locals left before HV troops arrived. We also were informed that on the evening of 6 August, the RSK attacked that platoon and took some materials and fuel and they were using a UN APC with a Red Cross symbol." [Interpretation] Mr. Marti, are you familiar with this event? Do you have any knowledge of it?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't have any knowledge of this event because it was not observed from my team.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I submit this portion of the report, 65 ter 0508 for admission into evidence with one reservation that it is possible that it has already been introduced as part of Exhibit P65; and I think this is something I need to clear up with my colleague from the Prosecution and with the Registrar, but I would like to propose that it be entered into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, perhaps if there are indeed differences between P68 and this document, we don't object maybe that specific page to enter as an exhibit and it's indeed correct that the witness has discussed this Exhibit 0508 in his witness statement which is now P417 at paragraphs 65 and 66.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So it was this copy that he ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Since there are no objections, you want to tender only this portion, Mr. Mikulicic or the whole of the document?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, there will be another few parts of that document that I will be referring to in further conversation, then maybe afterwards we could -- you could ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps it's easier since you are talking about differences in page numbering and what appears on the cover page because the witness answered questions about that as well that ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes. I have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That we receive it in evidence in it's entirety.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Okay. I was just informed by Mr. Kehoe that in P68, the paragraph that I'm referring to is on page 830, I'm referring to the ERN numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you are referring to the ERN numbers. You did that before when you referred to page 118.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: The different ERN numbers in that document as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But I think if we refer to pages, the protocol is that we refer to the pages within the document as uploaded in e-court and that would be the fifth page out of 35 for this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, could you assign a number to this?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit number D391.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D391 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed, Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And looking at the clock, I notice that you have 7 minutes left.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you for reminding me. I will do my best.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Marti, in this same document, we can find under the entry for the 28th of August, an event that relates to something that happened in the village Musica Stanovi. This Trial Chamber has already had occasion to hear that in this village, former soldiers of the army of Serbian Krajina were found, to be more precise, ten of them, and with the assistance of the special police, these soldiers were taken to Knin. Do you have any personal knowledge about this event, Mr. Marti?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have some knowledge because the day before, me and Alex Tchernetsky and me conducted a patrol, we wanted to proceed in this area where this village is in Podinarje and -- but then we saw that special -- by that time, we didn't know who was it but special unit was conducting a kind of investigation in the area, we saw many armed people going forwards to Podinarje area and then the next day, we conducted another patrol specially to this area but me, myself, was not on this patrol because I tasked Alex to do that patrol because me, I went in another direction. And in the evening, Alex and the other team member told me about the case what has happened, that means that this man wanted to be handed out to the Croatian authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the fact that when the special police arrived in the village, these former soldiers of the army of the Serbian Krajina surrendered to the special police with no weapons on them and at the same time, the Croatian police, special police found in the vicinity of this village, they found some weapons, a rifle and 6 AK-47 rifles, automatic rifles?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of these details but I remember after that case, there was one man and handed over, he said he's still afraid he has hidden somewhere a gun and he handed over this weapon to Alex but that was a single case. That was not during this case but he was afraid, he didn't want to -- that somebody else found this gun and he handed over this gun to Alex.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. In order to use the remaining time efficiently, I propose that pages 21 and 22 which refer to this event be introduced -- be tendered into evidence. These are pages from the document 65 ter 00508.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi, no objections? Mr. Mikulicic, we admitted the whole of it but if there is any specific reason why you want to have these two pages in addition to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: No, that's fine. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Now, to return to Exhibit P68 on page 36 of this exhibit, I will read a portion of this document: [In English] " ... info received," [Interpretation] this is an entry dated the 13th of September [In English] "Info received on 8 Serb soldiers who surrendered, the individuals are spread amongst the county court in Split and Zadar awaiting investigations." [Interpretation] Are you aware of this event of the 13th of September when eight soldiers surrendered, soldiers of the former army of the Republic of Serbian Krajina?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: They surrendered where?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [In English] It is written only "surrendered." [Interpretation] So I don't know where they surrendered. I was just asking you whether you knew about this event?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I only know about the surrendering in Podkonje.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: That was on the 28th of August and this was on the 13th of September?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mikulicic. That's what the witness tells us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That he only knows about the other occasion. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us proceed a bit more quickly. Are you aware, Mr. Marti, of the fact that Croatian authorities, and I mean the civilian and special police and the army, instances where they assisted the local population which remained in their villages after Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not very much. The only thing I note is that after a while, they established this system that everybody should get a new Croatian ID card and UN was helping to collect the remaining former Serb population and bringing them either to Knin or to Gracac to collect this ID card.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, I'm looking at the clock. Mr. Waespi, at this moment, would you need 14 minutes or could you do it in 12?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I do my best whatever time I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then the same is for you, one last question, Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I will end up by tendering the three incepts of this report from daily sitreps from 4 September until 4th October, and that is the examples of Croatian authorities to help the Serb population remaining on their villages after Operation Storm, and I am referring to page 35 of that document where it is said that: "UNMO patrol met an old lady in Donji Lapac who returned to her house on 10th September. And she states local police has given her enough food and water supply as required. The police will fix the electricity in her house on 13th September. She also informed UNMOs that she has no problems with local police or Croatian army and she would like to stay in Donji Lapac." The other example is from the very same document, on page 28 where it is said, "UNMO patrol observed 8 Serbs in Mala Popina, all are in good condition of health and were being helped with some food from two officers of a special police unit." And to that purpose I am only referring to the example which is written on page 34 in Selo Glogovo where it says that on 8 September visited the village Glogovo and provided food to Serbian civilians. Ten minutes after the patrol, a Croatian police patrol arrived and also provided the people with food which they stated they would be doing every second day."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: These are portions of the document that has been admitted what specific portions you would like to try and conclude.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And that concludes my examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Cayley, same as it was before.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: It's the same position, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. In fact, Mr. Cayley accedes the time he doesn't use to me. If Exhibit P419 could be please be brought up.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. Marti, I would like to raise just a few issues in re-examination. The first one relates back to the incidents of shelling on the 30th of July, 1995, and you marked yesterday the area B where you said the impact of the shells could be felt by you personally. Now, this morning you were asked by Mr. Kehoe about facilities partially military, partially MUP. Now, can you locate on this map where, if you can, you thought these facilities were located? And later mark it with letter E.

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It must be on the right side of the street but I don't -- I'm not sure if this map shows all the area. I would say here. I mean on the right side of the street so ...

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think we have a protocol in this Tribunal -- in this Trial Chamber that markings in blue are markings made at the request of the Defence and markings in red are made at the request of the Prosecution. So could we try to get -- which might not be easy because the blue is overlapping the -- oh, yes, the original remains. Could we now make this marking again but now in red, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it also moves a bit at the same time with the colour. Now, in order to avoid whatever confusion, the question mark was for the little circle and not for the larger one which is marked by an E, capital E. Mr. Waespi, any further marking needed?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then Mr. Registrar, the now again marked map on top of the earlier marking will be ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P427, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I can take it there is no objection against P427? Then P427 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now witness I think you also testified that there were I think five or six shells impacted in the area D; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Near the building as a shelter. We didn't know when the fire would stop so we just had to count.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you. At that time and given your experience in artillery on mortar, did you form an impression as to what the purpose was of these five to six shells?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, actually I -- according to my experience, I couldn't imagine that with such a procedure, you try to hit any military target. I mean if you are conducting artillery shelling, you have somewhere you have artillery observer, he tells you -- he tells the artillery unit exactly where they have to shoot and at least -- I mean in my experience as a mortar commander after the third shot, you should hit the target and not just shelling in different places. So me, I couldn't imagine by that time that that is a shelling exactly guided on a military target. And by the way, you still have to also to deal with what is around the military target. Of course nowadays, it's just called collateral damages, but that can also -- always means that this collateral damages are civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let's move on to the next issue. You were quoted this morning by Mr. Kehoe at page 34 from Colonel Hjertnes who said that there had been difficult time for some of the UNMOs to objectively assessing the shelling. In your personal opinion, were you one of the UNMOs who had difficulties because they were emotionally affected by the shelling in assessing the impact of the shelling?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean of course you are emotionally affected when the shelling is so close to you then you think is there an artillery observer and if he is observing, doesn't he see that there is a UN patrol on the way? So that -- that was of course it can cause a lot of emotions when you are -- when you feel that you are near an artillery fire or almost under fire yourself.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Did it affect your judgement in assessing the -- what you said shelling of civilian targets in Knin?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: My assessment about the shelling in Knin was that apart from this as I have learned today, this HQ in Knin, that there was not a real military target which you have to attack with artillery. I think I have mentioned it before. I mean to attack something with artillery, that means you must have a very large target and as a military commander, I think you should also be quite sure that you don't hit anything which doesn't belong to the target.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Turning to the issue of the perpetrators, the identity of the perpetrators, at page 43, you were asked about the difficulty to identify these perpetrators. Now, would it be easier for the military police and other law enforcement agencies, normal police, to identify perpetrators?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sure --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, with all due respect, I don't think he with speak for the military police, it would be easier for the military police or the civilian police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi, the witness has clearly expressed where his points of doubt were. He has done that even not once, but even twice in his statement and then later asked the same questions again. Now, to see whether others would have had it easier to do the same thing might not be within the factual knowledge of this witness. So therefore, if there's any factual elements you can ask him but not this kind of opinion or judgement. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, you testified that you expected the Croatian authorities to do more than what they did on the ground and there was also a question put to you about orders that might have been issued from Zagreb. Now, please tell the Court again what expectations you had at that time that the Croatian authorities should have done to control these perpetrators.

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: My expectation were that on the main crossing points, they should have -- they should by that time establish checkpoints. They should control who is coming in from -- through Drnis or from Vrlika or whatever, into the region and who is going back with which items took from the area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi, I think the witness told us already before the same thing. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you. No further questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Bench has no further questions. Has the re-examination triggered any need for further questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: One question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One question, Mr. Kehoe. Further cross-examination by Mr. Kehoe:

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: With regard to the shelling at Strmica, you noted at in P417 paragraph 28 with regard to the shelling, you noted that "there was a Serbian checkpoint nearby but I can't say what the target was meant to be." Is that accurate you don't know what the target was meant to be that was shot it, do you? If you can look at your statement, P417 paragraph 28?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my opinion, the checkpoint is not a target for artillery shelling.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Marti, this concludes your evidence in this court. I would like to thank you very much for having answered many, many questions put to you by the parties and by the Bench and if I would use your own language which I will now do, [German spoken].

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I just wished the witness a safe trip home again which might not have come as a surprise to you. We adjourn until tomorrow, the 11th of June, 9.00 in the morning, Courtroom III and Mr. Waespi, the Chamber fears that on Thursday, we'll have no witness and of course if the Chamber allots time to the Prosecution to present evidence, and if then days are not used, then we'll have to consider what the consequences are for the time allocated to the Prosecution because the time is there although no evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Yes, we'll look into that. We, as you know, still have two witnesses and -- but we -- yes, indeed, anticipate that these will be two rather short witnesses and we'll endeavour, perhaps, to find an additional witness. Mr. Steenbergen is unfortunately unavailable to come already this week. That's one attempt we made. And we'll continue doing that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. We stand adjourned until tomorrow morning, 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
